 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. For most of the Basque derby's history, Athletic Club has been the bigger club. It is the club traditionally known for having more fans, more money and the more famous identity. Heading into Sunday night's meeting at the iconic San Mamés on the banks of the Nervión River, the balance has shifted 60 miles down the Basque coastline from Bilbao towards San Sebastián.
 Heading into Sunday's derby, Real Sociedad sit fifth in LaLiga with 19 points, while Athletic are eighth with 12, although they have a game in hand. More telling is what happened last season, when La Real went four derbies unbeaten against their neighbours and knocked them out of the Copa del Rey on the way to winning it.
Much of that success was built at Zubieta, the club's training ground and academy. "A lot of good work is done there, and I was there since I was very young," said Jon Martín, the 20-year-old centre-back, speaking on a LaLiga media call with me ahead of the derby. "I started at the academy when I was 12, and gradually all the work you do helps you through each different phase."
 Jon Martín in action for Real Sociedad.
 Homegrown heroes in the derby
 The derby results last season showed what that work at Zubieta produces, with those who came through the ranks proving decisive. In November 2025, La Real won a five-goal thriller in the league beating Athletic 3-2 at Reale Arena, and the late winner came from Jon Gorrotxategi. He was 23 at the time and had been at the club since he was 15, hailing from the small town of Eibar just a short drive from San Sebastián. The return fixture at San Mamés in February finished 1-1.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement In the Copa del Rey semi-final, another academy graduate, Beñat Turrientes, scored the only goal of the first leg in Bilbao. Captain Mikel Oyarzabal, a Zubieta product who has spent his whole career at the club, converted an 87th-minute penalty in the second leg to seal a 2-0 aggregate win. Six weeks later, La Real beat Atlético Madrid on penalties in Seville to lift the trophy.
 For Martín, who has played in four or five derbies, being homegrown changes how the fixture feels. "It's not just a result, it's the feeling of being a member of the team," he said. "As I'm a homegrown player, well, I have great feelings for this, and I think we all face this match with tremendous passion."
 A changing tendency
 Zubieta's best graduates have always attracted the biggest clubs, and for much of this century, they have been tempted by the riches and glamour of a move away. World Cup winner Xabi Alonso came through the academy before eventually leaving for Liverpool in 2004. Another generational talent was Antoine Griezmann, spotted in France as a teenager, developed at Zubieta and broke into the first team before joining Atlético Madrid in 2014.
 Now Chelsea coach Xabi Alonso in action for his boyhood club against Barcelona.
 The departure that still hurts most went the shortest distance. Iñigo Martínez, a Zubieta-trained center-back, crossed to arch rivals Athletic in January 2018 after the Bilbao club paid his release clause. He was not the first player to make the move, but was the most important player to make the move since Joseba Etxeberria over 20 years before.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement More recently, Martín Zubimendi spent his whole career at La Real, making 236 appearances, before Arsenal paid close to €70 million ($78 million) for him in 2025. Arsenal have become a regular destination, and their coach, Mikel Arteta, is a former La Real player himself. In London, Zubimendi joined former team-mates Mikel Merino and Martin Ødegaard in north London, with the midfield trio having once operated in blue and white on a weekly basis.
 The Premier League's pull is mostly financial. When Liverpool and Arsenal chased Zubimendi and Merino in 2024, even La Real's improved contract offers could not match the wages available in England. Even so, the club did well to retain them for so long, with Zubimendi rejecting a move to Liverpool a year prior to stay in San Sebastián.
 Those who stay
 Some players turn the money down. Legendary former captain Xabi Prieto spent his entire career at La Real before retiring in 2018, and current captain Mikel Oyarzabal has followed the same road. In 2016, there was speculation that Athletic was ready to trigger Oyarzabal's €40 million ($45 million) release clause, but signed a new contract with La Real instead. When Barcelona were linked with him this summer, he told reporters that Real Sociedad and San Sebastián are his home. Even now, after scoring five goals in eight games to fire Spain to World Cup glory, he appears to be showing no sign of being tempted by a move away.
 Xabi Prieto spent his entire career with the club.
 Defender Jon Martín is next in line. He signed his third contract extension in two years in July, committing to the club until 2032, and reports put his release clause between €50 million and €60 million ($56 million to $67 million). When he renewed, he named three fellow homegrown talents, Oyarzabal, Igor Zubeldia and Ander Barrenetxea as the players he learns from.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Asked what the club had done to persuade him to commit so far ahead, Martín pointed to the same thing Oyarzabal does. "I've already always said that this is my home. I've been here since I was 12," he said. "At the end of the day, the feeling of belonging and to want to be here is something I feel from inside."
 He insisted that interest from bigger clubs is a compliment, not a distraction. "I always say that I'm very grateful for all these things and possible interest, because I think that I'm a player that people like," he said. "I don't pay too much notice of all these things that happen, because I'm playing for La Real. I feel it's my home and I have to focus on that."
 He also made clear that he believes the club can take him as far as he wants to go. "I feel this is my home, it's where I want to be, and I think everything I need to be able to perform at a top level is here at the club," he said.
 That ability to match his ambition is what has changed in San Sebastián. The likes of Alonso and Griezmann were forced to depart to compete in Europe, but Real Sociedad has qualified for continental action in six of the last 10 seasons, reaching the last 16 of the UEFA Champions League in 2024 before being eliminated by Paris Saint-Germain. Just last week, La Real beat Norwegian side Lillestrøm 6-0 in their own backyard in the Europa League.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Those they sign, develop and sell
 What separates La Real from Athletic is the third part of the model, as Athletic fields only players born or developed in the Basque Country, so it does not shop abroad. La Real can, and it has become expert at buying undervalued players, improving them and selling them on.
 Current Arsenal superstar Mikel Merino arrived from Newcastle in 2018 and left for Arsenal for about €33 million ($37 million) in 2024. Alexander Isak joined from Borussia Dortmund in 2019 and became the most expensive sale in the club's history when Newcastle paid around €70 million ($78 million) for him. Robin Le Normand, a Frenchman who developed through the club's reserve team, joined Atlético Madrid for around €35 million ($39 million) in 2024.
 Even loan players have flourished. Martin Ødegaard spent the 2019-20 season at Anoeta on loan from Real Madrid, propelling a career that until then had struggled to match its early promise, and is now Arsenal's captain.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The numbers show how central that trading is to the club's strategy. Over the last five seasons, player sales made up 19% of La Real's average operating revenue of €160 million ($179 million). Athletic averaged €145 million ($162 million) over the same period. That financial power difference can be crucial when both sides compete for signings in their territory.
 Martín is relaxed about how long that development takes, pointing to the fact that every player has their own process. "Some flourish earlier, some later," he said, "and I respect the different moments."
 Two German-school coaches
 While the roots of both teams' success lie in the valleys of the Basque Country, both dugouts have changed in the last year, and both have been filled from the Bundesliga.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Pellegrino Matarazzo, the New Jersey-born former Stuttgart and Hoffenheim coach, took over at La Real in December 2025 and won the Copa four months later. Martín credits him with giving young players room to grow. "He sees that we're a brave team and we like to do daring things," he said. "He's very close to us and he's a coach that we can really trust, and for young players like me, that's something that we really appreciate."
 Real Sociedad's coach Pellegrino Matarazzo and players celebrate with the Copa del Rey trophy at San Sebastian's town hall.
 Further west, Athletic hired Edin Terzić, who took Borussia Dortmund to the 2024 Champions League final, in May on a contract to 2028. He has said that watching footage of Athletic's 2024 Copa celebrations persuaded him to take the job. His start has been uneven, with a 4-0 win over Getafe last weekend followed by a 3-1 defeat at Levante, where homegrown defender Aymeric Laporte was sent off.
 Sunday's derby at San Mamés
 None of that guarantees anything at San Mamés. With a win and their game in hand, Terzić's side could be back within a point of La Real, in a derby where both sides compete in every sense, on and off the field.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Martín called it "a healthy rivalry," and said he goes into it the way his father has always told him to. "He always tells me to feel calm before this type of match," he said. It may be easier to say that when it's his team ahead in the league standings.
 Balancing that calm with the "tremendous passion" he referenced earlier will be pivotal. For the first time in a long while, Athletic Club may feel that the pressure is on them to need the result more. For La Real's homegrown talents, that suits them.
